fig1_carnot.svg: The reversible Carnot bounds between a cold reservoir $T_c=300$ K and a hot one $T_h$. The engine efficiency $\eta=1-T_c/T_h$ (carnot_efficiency, left axis) is zero when $T_h=T_c$ and climbs toward $1$ only as $T_h\to\infty$; the refrigerator and heat-pump coefficients of performance (carnot_cop_refrigerator / carnot_cop_heat_pump, right axis) instead diverge as $T_h\to T_c$ — moving heat across a vanishing gap is nearly free. No real device beats these limits.
fig2_temperature_from_entropy.svg: Temperature emerges from entropy. Feeding the ideal-gas entropy $S(U)=\tfrac32 Nk_B\ln U$ to temperature_from_entropy — a numerical $1/T=(\partial S/\partial U)_{V,N}$ — returns a temperature (circles) that is exactly linear in $U$, i.e. $U=\tfrac32 Nk_BT$ (line). The second law's definition of $T$ thus reproduces equipartition: each of the three translational degrees of freedom carries $\tfrac12 k_BT$.
